source.title: Confinement of color: open problems and perspectives.

accepted.question_text: In finite-temperature QCD with dynamical quarks, is the deconfining transition an order-disorder transition associated with an exact vacuum symmetry and a genuine order parameter, or is it only a crossover in which quantities related to free quarks, such as the quark abundance ratio n_q/n_p and the inclusive quark-production cross section σ_q, become extremely small in the low-temperature phase without being exactly zero? Equivalently, is color confinement an absolute property of the vacuum enforced by symmetry, or only a very strong dynamical suppression of free quarks across a crossover?

evidence.quote: The "natural " explanation is that nq and σq are strictly zero , or that confinement is an absolute property of vacuum based on symmetry.
An "unnatural" alternative also exists compatible with a crossover: nq and σq very small but not identically zero in the confined phase and there is no order parameter.

A fundamental issue to understand confinement in QCD is whether the deconfining transition is order -disorder or can be a crossover , i.e. whether confinement is an absolute property of the vacuum based on symmetry or is a dynamical change of physical quantities like nq of Eq(1) or σq of Eq(2) by several orders of magnitude across a crossover.

accepted.question_text: For QCD with two light quark flavors (N_f = 2), is the finite-temperature chiral transition first order or second order? In the scenario described in the paper, the answer depends on whether the axial U_A(1) symmetry is effectively restored below the chiral transition or only above it. This matters because a second-order chiral transition at zero quark mass would imply that the finite-mass line is a crossover, whereas a first-order chiral transition would allow the finite-mass deconfining transition to remain first order and hence compatible with an order-disorder picture of confinement.
accepted.context_brief: Order of the N_f=2 chiral transition

evidence.quote: The region below the line is conventionally called confined, the region above it deconfined. A renormalization group analysis [5] shows that the chiral transition is first order for Nf ≥ 3 and can be second order or first order for Nf = 2 , depending on the fact that UA(1) symmetry is restored below or above the chiral transition.

Up to now lattice results were not conclusive on this point. New data [6] indicate that the transition is more compatible with first order . This is a fundamental question for our understanding of confinement and deserves further study.

accepted.question_text: In full QCD with dynamical quarks, what operational definition or order parameter should be used to distinguish the confined phase from the deconfined phase? The usual Polyakov-line criterion works in the quenched theory because the Z_3 center symmetry is exact there, but with dynamical quarks that symmetry is explicitly broken and the confining string can break through quark-pair creation, so neither the Polyakov loop nor the chiral condensate is generically an exact order parameter at nonzero quark mass.
accepted.context_brief: Operational confinement criterion in full QCD

evidence.quote: The real problem, both on the lattice and in experiment, is to give an operational definition of confined and deconfined.

In the presence of dynamical quarks the symmetry Z3 is explicitly broken and the string breaks at large enough distances converting the energy into the formation of quark pairs. No clear criterion exists to define confined and deconfined.
At generic values of m neither < L > nor < ψψ¯ > are order parameters.

accepted.question_text: What is the correct dual description of QCD confinement: which dual symmetry is broken or realized in the confining vacuum, and which topological excitations are the relevant carriers of that dual order? More concretely, among candidates such as monopoles obtained through abelian projection and vortices associated with nontrivial topology, which excitations actually provide the mechanism of color confinement in 3+1 dimensions, and how should their symmetry properties be identified?

evidence.quote: The problem is then to identify the dual symmetry and the corresponding topological excitations.
Vortices could be relevant to confinement also in (3+1)d[11].
Understanding the relevant dual excitations and their symmetries amounts to under￾stand the mechanism of color confinement.

I think that a fair conclusion is that we do not know yet the dual excitations : we only know that they carry magnetic charge in all abelian projections, and that the confining vacuum is a dual superconductor in the confined phase , a property which disappears above the deconfining transition.

accepted.question_text: How important is the gauge-group center to the confinement mechanism, and what can be learned by comparing different gauge theories that share the same center or by studying confining gauge groups with no center, such as G_2? In particular, can direct comparisons across such theories determine whether center degrees of freedom, rather than some broader class of magnetic or topological excitations, are essential to confinement?

evidence.quote: An interesting recent development is the exploration of the role of the center in the process of confinement[23] to check the claim that vortices are the relevant excitations. In particular the gauge group G2 which has no center does confine color.

Direct investigation of the role of the center by comparison of different groups with the same center can provide useful information, as well as the study of confinement with gauge groups like G2 which have no center.
